author: maya-chen
title: Why Can't I Relax? When Your Body Doesn't Feel Safe
dek: Why can't I relax when nothing is wrong? What your body is doing when it doesn't feel safe, and a 1-to-3-minute humming practice to try tonight.
seo_title: Why Can't I Relax? When Your Body Doesn't Feel Safe
seo_description: Why can't I relax when I know I'm safe? A plain look at what your nervous system is doing, plus a gentle humming practice with step-by-step instructions.
pull_quote: A hum can be a way of telling your body what your mind already knows.
body_html:
It's late on an ordinary weeknight. The dishes are done, the house is quiet, and nothing is wrong. You know nothing is wrong. And still your jaw is set, your chest feels tight, and your mind keeps replaying a conversation from last week. Somewhere around the third replay, the question arrives: why can't I relax?

You have already told yourself the obvious thing: you are not in danger. Your body heard it and stayed braced anyway.

If you have ever asked yourself, Why can't I just relax?, I want you to hear this clearly: that question contains a false premise. You're not failing to relax. Your nervous system is doing exactly what it was built to do.

Why can't I relax when I know I'm safe?

Most advice for an anxious mind is aimed at the thinking part of you, the part that can reason, plan and recognize that a threat isn't real. That work matters. The alarm, though, runs in older, automatic parts of your nervous system, and they don't speak in thoughts. They speak in sensation. That may be why you can win the argument with yourself and still feel your chest bracing for impact.

Picture Priya, 38, a composite, not a real person. "I understand my anxiety," she says. "I know it's not rational. And I still wake up every morning with my heart pounding like I've already done something wrong." Her understanding is real. It hasn't reached the part of her that sounds the alarm.

Your body does most of the talking

The vagus nerve is a long nerve that links your brain with your heart, lungs and gut. Most of its traffic runs upward: about 80 to 90 percent of the fibers in the vagus nerve carry signals from the body up to the brain (Breit et al., 2018).

The vagus nerve is the principal relay for sensory information from your lungs, windpipe and voice box, and its sensory fibers are the main sensory supply to your heart (Prescott & Liberles, 2022). So how you are breathing and how your heart is beating are part of what your brain is working with.

When your breath is quick and shallow and your shoulders are up, your brain may be listening to a body that is still reporting trouble. Giving your body something different to report is another way in.

Where this fits in nervous system regulation

Nervous system regulation is an everyday phrase for how your body moves into a stress response and finds its way back out. The best-known map of it comes from polyvagal theory, which Stephen Porges first set out in a 1994 presidential address, published in 1995. It describes three circuits: ventral vagal, sympathetic and dorsal vagal (Porges, 2022). It is a theory, and scientists still debate its premises (Grossman, 2023).

You may recognize yourself swinging between the last two, wired at midnight and flat and heavy by noon, with only short visits to the first. Nervous system regulation for beginners describes the three states in everyday terms and gives you a 3-minute check-in for finding where you are.

Nobody told your body the emergency was over

Think of a smoke detector installed too close to the stove. It goes off when you make toast. The detector works. It was set for a level of danger that made sense somewhere else, and nobody has reset it.

You never decided to stay on alert. At some point, maybe during a long stretch of stress, your body may have learned that staying ready felt safer than being caught off guard. That learning kept you going. As I put it in the book: "The problem isn't that your nervous system made the wrong call. The problem is that nobody ever told it the emergency was over."

So the job tonight is smaller than "relax." It is to send one signal from the body upward, in a language your body uses. A hum can be a way of telling your body what your mind already knows.

A hum can be a way of telling your body what your mind already knows.

A practice that skips the argument: humming

Humming needs no counting and no convincing. It stretches out your exhale without your having to manage it. And it gives you a vibration you can feel in your throat and chest, so your attention has somewhere to rest other than last week's conversation.

The evidence is preliminary. In a 2013 study, healthy young people hummed a single tone, sang a hymn and sang a slow mantra, and singing in regular phrases brought their heart rate into step with their breathing (Vickhoff et al., 2013). That finding is about heart rhythm and singing. I don't take it as evidence that a minute of humming will quiet anxiety.

A safety note first: most people need no special precautions for this one. If you have a vocal cord injury or have had recent throat surgery, check with your doctor first. If turning your attention inward tends to leave you floaty or disconnected, keep your eyes open and go slowly. If you feel lightheaded, stop humming and breathe normally.

Find a comfortable seat. The whole practice takes 1 to 3 minutes.

  1. Settle. Sit comfortably and close your mouth. Take a normal breath in through your nose.
  2. Start the hum. As you exhale, begin humming any single tone, the one that feels most natural. The pitch doesn't matter. Keep the vibration continuous and steady.
  3. Feel it. Notice the vibration in your lips, your throat and your chest. Place one hand on your breastbone to feel it more clearly.
  4. Follow the breath. Hum for the entire length of your exhale. Breathe in through your nose. Hum out again.
  5. Repeat. Continue for 6 to 10 breath cycles, about 1 to 2 minutes.
  6. Listen. After your last hum, sit in silence for 10 to 15 seconds. Notice what has changed.

If humming out loud isn't possible where you are, make a long, quiet "mmm" on each exhale with your lips barely parted.

Humming is Exercise 4 of the 27 in my book, Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety. The book also stretches it into a five-minute daily version, and it has a sequence for the 3 a.m. wake-up, for the nights when the replay starts after you've already been asleep.

What you might notice

You might feel the vibration spread from your throat into your chest and the bones of your face. There may be a little warmth or tingling in your face, or an urge to yawn or sigh at the end. You might feel self-conscious. That's normal, and the practice doesn't need to feel dignified.

You might also notice nothing. That is a common first result and it doesn't mean you did it wrong. If the hum makes you feel more on edge, stop, look around the room and name five things you can see.

When to use it

  • Late at night, when the replay starts and reasoning with it has stopped working.
  • In the car, before you walk into the house or the office.
  • In the shower, on a morning when you wake up already braced.

This week, when you close your laptop and notice your jaw is still set, try three hummed exhales before you stand up. Then notice what your nervous system does.

A hum is also a long breath out in disguise. If you would rather work with the breath directly, here are two breathing exercises to calm down when you're stressed. At bedtime, humming is one step of the longer exhale wind-down.

Questions women ask about "why can't I relax"

Why can't I relax even when nothing is wrong? The alarm runs in older, automatic parts of your nervous system, and they speak in sensation, not in thoughts. That may be why you can know you are safe and still feel your chest bracing. You're not failing to relax.

How long does the humming practice take? The whole practice takes 1 to 3 minutes: 6 to 10 hummed breaths, about 1 to 2 minutes, then 10 to 15 seconds of silence. You might notice nothing the first time. That is a common first result and it doesn't mean you did it wrong.

Does humming help with anxiety? I can't promise that it will. The evidence is preliminary, and the 2013 study behind this practice was about singing and heart rhythm, not anxiety. If your symptoms are new or keep coming back, a doctor can check that a physical problem isn't behind them.

These practices are meant to sit alongside professional care. They don't replace it. If your symptoms are new or keep coming back, a doctor can check that a physical problem isn't behind them. If you take medication for anxiety, please talk with your doctor before changing anything.

The opening scene and the humming exercise both come from my book, Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety. It has more practices like this one, each with its steps and an honest note on the evidence behind it.
source: Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety, Chapters 1 and 2, and Chapter 3 (Exercise 4, Humming)

author: maya-chen
title: Breathing Exercises for Sleep: The Longer Exhale at Bedtime
dek: Breathing exercises for sleep that fit around your toothbrush: a 4-minute wind-down with a longer exhale, then a low hum.
seo_title: Breathing Exercises for Sleep: The Longer Exhale at Bedtime
seo_description: Breathing exercises for sleep, step by step: in for 4, out for 8, then two minutes of humming. A gentle 4-minute wind-down for bedtime.
pull_quote: The key is that the exhale is longer than the inhale.
body_html:
It's 10:40 at night. You've been tired since the middle of the afternoon, and now that you're standing in the bathroom with the light on, your mind is wide awake. It's replaying the call you handled badly and sorting tomorrow's list. You're exhausted, but you can't turn off.

If you've gone looking for breathing exercises for sleep on a night like this, here is one that fits around brushing your teeth: a 4-minute wind-down, with two minutes of breathing on a longer exhale and then two minutes of humming.

Many people describe this same gap between tired and rested. One way to picture it: your body hasn't received a signal that the day is done. The dishes, the phone and the overhead lights all say keep going. An evening practice is a way to send that signal on purpose.

Why breathing exercises for sleep lean on the exhale

Your heart speeds up slightly as you breathe in and slows slightly as you breathe out. The name for that rhythm is respiratory sinus arrhythmia, and your vagus nerve is part of it (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014). A longer exhale means you spend more of each breath in the slowing half. That is the plain logic behind "in for 4, out for 8."

The research on the ratio itself is mixed. In a small 2014 experiment with 30 people, Van Diest and colleagues found that people reported more relaxation when the exhale was the longer part of the breath than when the inhale was. In 2024, Meehan and Shaffer compared a 1:2 ratio with even breaths at six breaths a minute and found no difference in heart rate variability.

Neither study measured sleep. Take this breath as a way to slow down at the end of the day, with no promise about how fast you'll drift off. I go through both studies in two breathing exercises to calm down when you're stressed, the daytime version of this breath.

You don't need to hit a perfect number. The key is that the exhale is longer than the inhale.

The key is that the exhale is longer than the inhale.

Why the second half is a hum

A hum is a long exhale with sound in it. You can't hum without letting your breath out slowly, so it keeps the longer exhale going while your hands are busy with pajamas and covers.

In one 2013 study, healthy young adults hummed a tone, sang a hymn and sang a slow mantra, and singing with a regular structure brought their heart rate into step with their breathing (Vickhoff et al., 2013). That study was about singing and it didn't look at sleep, so hold it loosely.

If counting your breath tends to wind you up, humming gives you a slow exhale with no numbers in it. On those nights you can just hum: mouth closed, a low note, 2 minutes.

Before you begin

A safety note: if you have asthma or COPD, check with your physician before practicing extended exhale breathing. If you're prone to lightheadedness or hyperventilation, go slowly and shorten the exhale at first. If you feel dizzy, return to normal breathing right away. And if you carry trauma or tend to dissociate, breathwork can occasionally feel activating rather than settling. You can stop and breathe naturally at any point.

If counting or watching your breath raises your anxiety, skip the breathing step and use the humming on its own for the first week. Humming alone is a complete evening practice. If you have a vocal cord injury or recent throat surgery, check with your physician before humming.

The 4-minute wind-down, step by step

Sit on the edge of your bed or on a bathroom stool. The practice itself takes 4 minutes: 2 minutes of breathing and 2 minutes of humming. Brushing your teeth in the middle and the three closing breaths in bed aren't counted, so allow a few minutes more on the clock.

  1. Settle. Feel your feet on the floor. Take one breath without managing it, and notice its quality: is it shallow, held or rapid?
  2. Breathe in for 4, out for 8. Inhale through your nose for 4 slow counts. Exhale through your nose or slightly parted lips for 8 slow counts. If 8 feels strained, use 6. Keep your jaw soft and let your hands rest open on your thighs. Continue for 2 minutes, roughly 8 to 10 cycles.
  3. Brush your teeth. Let your breath find its own pace while you brush, slow if that comes easily. No humming yet.
  4. Hum. Put the toothbrush away, close your mouth and hum on a comfortable low note: a song, a single tone or a simple "hmmmm." Breathe in through your nose whenever you need to. Feel the vibration in your chest and throat. Continue for 2 minutes while you change, fold back the covers and dim the lights.
  5. Close. Lie down and take three slow breaths with a long exhale. Set your phone face down or outside the room. Notice the weight of your body against the mattress. Rest.

The evening version in my book uses 4 in and 8 out, with 6 as the fallback, so the exhale can sit anywhere from 6 to 8 counts. If this breath is new to you, start at 4 in and 6 out, which is where the daytime version starts, and move to 8 once that feels easy. Leave the inhale at 4. If any count feels forced, drop to 4 in and 5 out and build from there.

This wind-down is one half of a daily routine in my book, Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety. The book adds the six-minute morning sequence and a 28-day log where you rate your anxiety from 0 to 5 each day, so you can see on paper whether anything is shifting.

What you might notice

Your thoughts may slow down during the humming, or your arms and legs may feel heavy. Restlessness or an urge to check your phone can show up too, and it may ease if you stay with the hum a little longer.

Sometimes sadness or warmth surfaces when the day finally goes quiet. You can let it be there, and if it feels like too much, open your eyes, stop and breathe normally.

You might also notice nothing. The book asks you to come back after 3 evenings and see what is different about falling asleep, even slightly, and it counts "nothing" and "I keep forgetting" as useful answers.

If lying flat is uncomfortable, the closing breaths work propped on pillows or in a recliner. If you feel self-conscious humming near a partner, keep it barely audible. A quiet hum still stretches out your exhale. And if the breathing leaves you dizzy or short of air, go back to normal breathing, then try a shorter exhale or the humming alone tomorrow.

When to use it

  • At your toothbrush, every night. The breathing goes just before you brush and the humming just after.
  • In bed, on the nights you forgot. You can do it lying down, half asleep. On the hardest days, 2 minutes of humming before sleep is enough to keep the habit alive.
  • When you wake in the small hours. The same breath works lying down in the dark: in for 4, out for 8, before you reach for your phone or check the time.

For the nights you're already lying down with the lamp off, there are three vagus nerve exercises in bed: a fist squeeze, a jaw-to-heels release and a quiet hum.

This wind-down is the evening half of a 10-minute daily routine in the book: six minutes in the morning, tied to your coffee, and four at night, tied to your toothbrush. If you're new to all of this and want a map first, start with nervous system regulation for beginners.

The morning half, six minutes with your coffee, is in a 10-minute daily vagus nerve routine.

Questions women ask about breathing exercises for sleep

How long should breathing exercises for sleep take? This one takes 4 minutes: 2 minutes of breathing in for 4 and out for 8, then 2 minutes of humming. On the hardest days, 2 minutes of humming before sleep is enough to keep the habit alive.

Can I do breathing exercises for sleep lying down? Yes. The breath works lying down in the dark, and on the nights you forgot you can do the wind-down in bed, half asleep. If lying flat is uncomfortable, try the closing breaths propped on pillows or in a recliner.

Will a longer exhale help me fall asleep faster? I can't promise that. The research on the ratio is mixed, and neither study measured sleep. Take this breath as a way to slow down at the end of the day, and if poor sleep keeps coming back, a doctor can check whether something physical is behind it.

These practices are meant to support professional care, not replace it. If poor sleep keeps coming back, a doctor can check whether something physical is behind it. If you take medication for anxiety or sleep, please talk with your doctor before changing anything.

The full morning and evening routine is in my book Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety, if you'd like to go further.

author: maya-chen
title: Nervous System Regulation for Beginners: A 3-Minute Start
dek: New to nervous system regulation? Learn what it means, the three states polyvagal theory describes, and a gentle 3-minute check-in to try today.
seo_title: Nervous System Regulation for Beginners: A 3-Minute Start
seo_description: New to nervous system regulation? Learn what it means, the three states polyvagal theory describes, and a gentle 3-minute check-in to try today.
pull_quote: None of these states is your fault. All of them are information.
body_html:
It's the middle of an ordinary day. Nothing is wrong, your inbox is under control, and your shoulders are still up near your ears. You sit down to rest and your body doesn't come with you. Somewhere you read that you need nervous system regulation, and you nodded, and you have no idea what to do with that.

Let's start there, because the phrase gets used far more often than it gets explained. If you're a beginner, you only need two things today: a rough map of the states your body moves through, and one small way of checking where you are.

What nervous system regulation means

Nervous system regulation is a loose, everyday phrase for how your body moves into a stress response and finds its way back out. It doesn't mean feeling calm all day, and it doesn't mean you stop getting activated. It means you stop staying there.

And if you've been stuck for a long time, please hear this: your nervous system isn't broken. It's been protecting you with the tools it had. The work now is giving it better ones.

Three states, as polyvagal theory maps them

The most familiar map comes from polyvagal theory, which Stephen Porges first set out in a 1994 presidential address, published in 1995. It describes three circuits in the autonomic nervous system, each tied to a different state (Porges, 2022). In everyday terms, they might feel like this:

Ventral vagal is safety and connection. Your breathing is easy, conversation feels natural, and problems feel solvable.

Sympathetic is fight or flight. Your heart works harder than the situation requires, your thoughts speed up, and your jaw, shoulders and belly brace without asking you first.

Dorsal vagal is shutdown. The world goes grey, flat and far away. You feel heavy and slow.

These are positions, not personality types.

In the theory, the sympathetic and dorsal responses are ways of surviving threat, so nobody is asking you to get rid of them. None of these states is your fault. All of them are information. The goal is more time in ventral, and an easier road back to it.

None of these states is your fault. All of them are information.

I want to be honest about the map, too. Polyvagal theory is a theory, and scientists still debate it. In a 2023 paper, the researcher Paul Grossman argued that each of its basic premises is "either untenable or highly implausible." Porges, for his part, has kept refining the theory and responding to its critics (Porges, 2025). So hold the three states as words for noticing your body, not as settled anatomy.

Why regulation starts in the body

Your vagus nerve is one of the main lines between your organs and your brain, and much of its traffic runs upward. It is the principal relay for sensory information from your lungs, and its sensory fibers are the main sensory supply to your heart (Prescott & Liberles, 2022).

So how you're breathing and how your heart is beating are part of what your brain is working with. If someone has ever told you to calm down and nothing happened, you already know that telling doesn't reach everything. Thinking work is valuable and it has its place. The body is simply another way in.

It's hard to change what you can't notice, which makes a check-in a kind place for a beginner to start.

The Nervous System Check-In, step by step

This is a practice from my book, a way of paying attention. It isn't a tested clinical protocol.

A safety note first: if you carry a trauma history or tend to feel floaty or disconnected when you turn your attention inward, go slowly. Keep your eyes open if closed eyes feel unsafe, and pause to look around the room any time it feels like too much.

Find a comfortable seat with your feet flat on the floor, or lie down if that's easier. The whole practice takes about 2 to 3 minutes. Give each of the first six steps about 10 seconds.

  1. Settle. Place both hands in your lap, palms up. Take one normal breath and notice it without changing it.
  2. Jaw. Is it clenched or easy? Notice whether your teeth are touching. No fixing yet.
  3. Shoulders. Are they lifted toward your ears?
  4. Belly. Is it soft or braced? Does your breath reach your lower abdomen, or does it stop at your chest?
  5. Heart area. Is there tightness, heaviness, openness or warmth? Put a word or a color to it, whatever arrives first.
  6. Name it. Which state are you closest to right now: ventral, sympathetic or dorsal? Just name it, with no judgment.
  7. Exhale. Take one slow breath out through slightly parted lips, longer than your inhale. Feel your shoulders drop even a millimeter. Return to the room.

The check-in is the first exercise in my book, Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety, where it comes with a journal prompt for writing down what you noticed. From there the book moves on to 27 exercises in three tiers, each with a note on how strong its evidence is.

What you might notice

You might be surprised by how much tension you're carrying. That isn't something to fix right now. You might struggle to locate any sensation at all, and that's allowed too. A small wave of emotion can surface as well.

If sitting upright is uncomfortable, try this on your back with your knees bent and your feet flat on the floor. If you feel overwhelmed or very floaty, open your eyes, look around the room and name five things you can see before you continue.

The check-in ends on one long breath out, and if you'd like to stay with that breath at night, these breathing exercises for sleep build a 4-minute bedtime wind-down around it.

What regulation can feel like

It doesn't have to feel like bliss. It might be a small release of breath, your shoulders dropping half an inch, a moment of quiet between thoughts. Deb Dana calls these glimmers, "micro-moments of regulation that foster feelings of well-being," and part of this practice is learning to catch them before they pass unnoticed.

The first run doesn't make you a runner, but the first run still counts.

If you'd like a simple way to begin, try checking in three times today: morning, midday and evening. And this week, when a difficult email arrives and your chest tightens before you've finished reading, bring your attention to your exhale. One extended breath out, as slow as you can make it. Notice what your nervous system does.

Questions women ask about nervous system regulation for beginners

What does nervous system regulation mean? It is a loose, everyday phrase for how your body moves into a stress response and finds its way back out. It doesn't mean feeling calm all day, and it doesn't mean you stop getting activated.

How long does it take to regulate your nervous system? It varies, and I can't give you a timeline. The check-in itself takes about 2 to 3 minutes, and it is a way of paying attention to where you are. Regulation may show up as something small, such as a release of breath or your shoulders dropping half an inch.

How often should a beginner do the check-in? A simple way to begin is three times today: morning, midday and evening. Each check-in takes about 2 to 3 minutes. If you carry a trauma history or tend to feel floaty when you turn your attention inward, go slowly and keep your eyes open.

These practices are meant to support professional care, not replace it. If you take medication for anxiety, please talk with your doctor before changing anything.

If you want to understand more of the why, read why your body doesn't believe you're safe. For something to do with your breath, try two breathing exercises for when you're stressed. And if you'd like to see what my book Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety is like before anything else, you can peek inside at a full practice from it.
source: Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety, Chapters 1, 2 and 3 (Exercise 01, The Nervous System Check-In)

author: maya-chen
title: Breathing Exercises to Calm Down When You're Stressed
dek: Two breathing exercises to calm down when stress spikes: a sigh for under a minute, a slow exhale for three, and what the research really shows.
seo_title: Breathing Exercises to Calm Down When You're Stressed
seo_description: Two breathing exercises to calm down when stress spikes: a sigh for under a minute, a slow exhale for three, and what the research really shows.
body_html:
It's 11:47 in the morning and you're about to walk into a meeting you've been dreading. Your jaw is clenched, your shoulders are somewhere near your ears, and your heart has already decided this is an emergency. You don't have ten minutes for a breathing session. You have ninety seconds in a bathroom stall.

Someone has probably told you to take a deep breath. It's kind advice and it doesn't tell you much. How long? In through what? These two breathing exercises to calm down come with the actual steps: one for when you have under a minute, one for when you have three.

Being stressed in your body doesn't mean you're handling your life badly.

What a breathing exercise can and can't do

Slow, deliberate breathing can help some people feel less stressed. In a 2023 meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials, Fincham and colleagues linked breathwork with lower self-reported stress than control conditions, and the effect held in the ten trials of slow-paced breathing. The effect was small to medium, and the authors asked readers to interpret it cautiously.

The results weren't significant for groups living with mental or physical health conditions, though their numbers were close to the others, and the authors say that may reflect how few people were studied.

Think of these two practices as circuit breakers, not renovations.

Circuit breakers, not renovations.

Why your breath is worth working with

Your heart speeds up slightly as you inhale and slows slightly as you exhale. The name for that rhythm is respiratory sinus arrhythmia, and your vagus nerve is part of it (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014).

A longer exhale is often sold as the whole secret. The research is less tidy. In a small 2014 experiment with 30 people, Van Diest and colleagues found that breathing out for more than twice as long as breathing in led people to report more relaxation than the reverse pattern. In 2024, Meehan and Shaffer measured heart rate variability at six breaths a minute and found a 1:2 ratio did no better than even breaths, and the earlier studies they reviewed disagreed with each other. They measured different things, so nobody has the last word.

Take the long exhale as an invitation and not a formula. If it steadies you, keep it. If even breaths feel better, that counts.

Before you begin

A safety note: if you have asthma or COPD, check with your physician before practicing extended exhale breathing. If you're prone to lightheadedness or hyperventilation, go slowly and shorten the exhale at first. If you feel dizzy, return to normal breathing right away. And if you carry trauma or tend to dissociate, breathwork can occasionally feel activating rather than settling. You can stop and breathe naturally at any point.

Practice one: the physiological sigh

This is the one for the bathroom stall. It's a double inhale through the nose followed by a long, slow exhale. Sighing isn't foreign to your body, either: sighs happen on their own every few minutes to re-inflate the tiny air sacs in your lungs (Li et al., 2016).

Here's what the study actually did. In a 2023 randomized trial from Stanford (Balban et al., Cell Reports Medicine), 108 people, mostly undergraduates, spent five minutes a day for a month on one of four practices: cyclic sighing, box breathing, cyclic hyperventilation or mindfulness meditation. All four groups felt less anxious after their daily session. Cyclic sighing brought a bigger lift in positive mood than mindfulness, and a bigger drop in breathing rate. On anxiety, breathwork and mindfulness came out about even, and heart rate variability didn't differ between the groups. The authors describe the study as exploratory, and it was too small to rank the breathing styles against each other.

The version below is much shorter than what they tested, so think of it as a quick taste of the practice.

Find a seated or standing position. This takes 30 to 60 seconds.

  1. Inhale fully through your nose for 4 counts.
  2. Without exhaling, take a second, shorter sniff on top of the first, as if you're topping off a nearly full glass.
  3. Exhale slowly and completely through your mouth, lips slightly parted, for 6 to 8 counts. Let your shoulders drop on the way out.
  4. Pause naturally at the bottom of the exhale for 1 to 2 seconds.
  5. Return to normal breathing and notice the quality of your next few breaths.

You can repeat up to 3 cycles. If the double inhale feels uncomfortable, try a single full inhale followed by the long exhale. If you need to be quiet, exhale through your nose; people in the Stanford trial could breathe entirely through the nose.

Practice two: the longer exhale

This is the one for when you have a few minutes.

Find a comfortable seated position. This takes 1 to 3 minutes.

  1. Place one hand on your belly and let it rest there, without pressing.
  2. Inhale through your nose for 4 counts. Feel your belly rise before your chest.
  3. Without pausing, exhale slowly through slightly parted lips for 6 counts.
  4. If that feels comfortable after a few cycles, extend the exhale to 8 counts. Leave the inhale at 4.
  5. Continue for 6 to 10 breath cycles and let the rhythm become automatic.
  6. Return to your natural breath and notice how things feel now.

If counting feels like too much when you're stressed, whisper a long "shhhh" on the exhale instead.

These are Exercises 1 and 3 of the 27 in my book, Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety. For the times you can't step out at all, it has three discreet tools you can use in the meeting itself, and for a spike, a 90-second sequence in three steps: orient, regulate, reanchor.

What you might notice

Your shoulders or jaw may feel heavier. You might yawn or sigh without meaning to, or feel a little drowsy. Feeling nothing is also normal, and a quiet first try doesn't tell you much: in the Stanford trial, the lift in mood from sighing grew the more days people kept at it. If the count feels forced, drop to 4 in and 5 out and build from there.

If your breath slows and the rest of you stays braced, read why can't I relax when I know I'm safe, which adds a humming practice that needs no counting.

This week, when a difficult call ends and you're still holding the phone, bring your attention to your shoulders. Try one physiological sigh before you do anything else. Then notice what your nervous system does.

Questions women ask about breathing exercises to calm down

How long do breathing exercises take to calm you down? The physiological sigh takes 30 to 60 seconds and the longer exhale takes 1 to 3 minutes. What you feel afterward varies, and feeling nothing on a first try is normal. In the Stanford trial, the lift in mood from sighing grew the more days people kept at it.

Do breathing exercises really help with stress? They can help some people feel less stressed. A 2023 meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials linked breathwork with lower self-reported stress than control conditions, with a small to medium effect that the authors asked readers to interpret cautiously. Think of these two as circuit breakers, not renovations.

Are breathing exercises safe for everyone? Some people need a check first. If you have asthma or COPD, talk with your physician before practicing extended exhale breathing, and if you're prone to lightheadedness or hyperventilation, go slowly and shorten the exhale. If you feel dizzy, return to normal breathing right away.

These practices are meant to support professional care, not replace it. If your symptoms are new or keep coming back, a doctor can check that a physical problem isn't behind them. If you take medication for anxiety, please talk with your doctor before changing anything.

If the evenings are your hardest time, the longer exhale at bedtime adapts this same breath for winding down. If you're not sure where to begin, start with nervous system regulation for beginners. And if you'd like to see what my book Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety is like, you can peek inside at a full practice from it.

title: Vagus Nerve Exercises You Can Do in Bed
dek: Three vagus nerve exercises you can do in bed, lying down in the dark: a fist squeeze, a jaw-to-heels release and a quiet hum. About 3 to 4 minutes.
seo_title: Vagus Nerve Exercises You Can Do in Bed
seo_description: Vagus nerve exercises in bed, step by step: three quiet practices for bedtime or the 3 a.m. wake-up, with timings and an honest note on the evidence.
pull_quote: Start with whatever is already clenched.
body_html:
It's 11:20 and the lamp has been off for half an hour. Beside you, someone is breathing the slow breath of a person who fell asleep in four minutes. You are flat on your back with your jaw set and your hands curled, running tomorrow's meeting for the third time. Getting up would wake the house.

Most vagus nerve exercises you'll find ask for a chair, a sink of cold water or a voice at full volume. The three vagus nerve exercises in bed below are done lying down, in the dark, quietly enough that the person next to you keeps sleeping.

What vagus nerve exercises in bed can and can't do

The vagus nerve is a long nerve that links your brain with your heart, lungs and gut. It is the principal relay for sensory information from your lungs, windpipe and voice box (Prescott & Liberles, 2022). So how you are breathing is part of what your brain is working with.

"Vagus nerve exercises" is a popular, loose name for practices like the ones below. I can't point you to research that tested any of them in bed or measured sleep. They come from my book as practices: small, physical things to do with a body that is still braced. They may help you settle. They come with no promise about sleep.

Picture Carmen, 41, a composite, not a real person. She knows the meeting will go fine, and her hands are fists under the blanket anyway. Start with whatever is already clenched.

Start with whatever is already clenched.

Before you begin

A safety note: the third exercise is a long exhale. If you have asthma, COPD or another breathing condition, check with your physician before practicing it. If you feel dizzy or lightheaded, return to normal breathing right away. If paying attention to your breath tends to raise your anxiety, skip the hum and stay with the first two exercises. And if you carry trauma or tend to dissociate, lying still in the dark can feel activating rather than settling. Keep your eyes open, and at any point you can stop and breathe normally.

If you have a vocal cord injury or have had recent throat surgery, check with your physician before humming. If you have pain, an injury or arthritis in your hands or wrists, skip the fist squeeze. It should be firm and never painful.

Exercise 1: the fist squeeze

Tensing a muscle on purpose and then letting it go comes from progressive relaxation, a method the physician Edmund Jacobson developed in the early twentieth century (Jacobson, 1929). The book borrows that one move for the hands, on the idea that a release is easier to feel right after a squeeze. I have no study of this short version to offer.

Stay as you are, on your back or your side. This takes about 30 seconds.

  1. Squeeze. Close both hands into fists at about 70 percent of your full grip.
  2. Hold for 7 seconds. Keep breathing while you hold.
  3. Release completely. Let your fingers spread and your palms go soft.
  4. Feel the weight of your hands on the sheet or on your belly for 10 seconds.

One squeeze is the whole exercise.

Exercise 2: jaw, shoulders, heels

This one comes from the book's sequence for waking at 3 a.m. I know of no research on it as a set. It is a way of checking, in order, the places that tend to brace. Allow about 1 minute.

  1. Look. Keep your eyes open and let your gaze go soft. Find two or three shapes you can see in the dark. You are in your room.
  2. Jaw. Let your back teeth come slightly apart and let your tongue drop away from the roof of your mouth. Keep your lips gently closed. Stay there for 10 seconds.
  3. Shoulders. Let them drop away from your ears and into the mattress. Stay for 10 seconds.
  4. Hands. Check them. If they have closed again, let them open.
  5. Heels. Press both heels into the mattress. Feel the weight and the pressure, then ease off.

Exercise 3: the quiet hum

A hum is a long exhale with sound in it. Your heart rate tends to rise after you breathe in and fall after you breathe out (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014), which is the plain logic behind practices that lean on the exhale.

The evidence for humming itself is preliminary. In a 2013 study, healthy young people hummed a single tone, sang a hymn and sang a slow mantra, and singing in regular phrases brought their heart rate into step with their breathing (Vickhoff et al., 2013). That study was about singing and it didn't look at sleep, so hold it loosely.

The bed version is the book's quiet variation: a long "mmm" with your lips barely parted. It takes 1 to 2 minutes.

  1. Breathe in normally through your nose.
  2. Hum out. As you exhale, make a quiet "mmm" on any single tone, for the whole length of the breath.
  3. Feel it. Rest one hand on your breastbone and notice the vibration in your lips, your throat and your chest.
  4. Repeat for 6 to 10 breaths, about 1 to 2 minutes.
  5. Listen. After your last hum, lie in silence for 10 to 15 seconds.

The seated, full-voice version is in why you can't relax when your body doesn't feel safe.

The in-bed sequence, start to finish

  1. Fist squeeze, about 30 seconds: 70 percent grip, 7 seconds, release.
  2. Jaw, shoulders, heels, about 1 minute: 10 seconds for the jaw, 10 for the shoulders, hands open, heels pressed.
  3. Quiet hum, 1 to 2 minutes: 6 to 10 hummed exhales, then 10 to 15 seconds of silence.

That adds up to about 3 minutes with six hums and closer to 4 with ten.

The fist squeeze and the jaw release come from the chapter on anxiety spikes in my book, Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety. There, the squeeze is one of three discreet tools for moments when you can't step away, such as a meeting, alongside a 90-second sequence for a spike.

The book's own 3 a.m. sequence has two breathing steps that I've left out, because each has its own entry. One is a double inhale with a long exhale, done twice. The steps are in two breathing exercises to calm down when you're stressed. The other is in for 4, out for 8, which the book suggests for 3 minutes if you are still wide awake afterward. It is the center of the longer exhale at bedtime. The book's rule for the night applies here too: don't check the time until you have finished.

And if the words around all of this are new to you, nervous system regulation for beginners gives you a plain map of the three states and a 3-minute check-in.

What you might notice

Your hands may feel warm or heavy after the squeeze. You might yawn or sigh, or feel the hum in your chest and the bones of your face.

You might also notice nothing. That is a common first result. Feeling more awake at first can happen too. Paying attention to your body can leave you more alert for a few minutes.

If any of it leaves you more on edge, floaty or short of air, stop. Open your eyes, breathe normally and name five things you can see.

When to use it

  • Falling asleep, when the lamp is off and your mind is still at work. Start with the fists.
  • At the 3 a.m. wake-up, before you reach for your phone. Begin with the shapes in the dark, then the jaw.
  • On a weekend morning, before you get up, when you wake already braced.

Questions women ask about vagus nerve exercises in bed

Can you do vagus nerve exercises lying down? You can do these three lying down, in the dark, without getting up. They are quiet enough that the person next to you keeps sleeping.

How long do vagus nerve exercises in bed take? About 3 minutes with six hums and closer to 4 with ten. The fist squeeze takes about 30 seconds, the jaw, shoulders and heels about 1 minute, and the quiet hum 1 to 2 minutes.

Do vagus nerve exercises help you sleep? I can't promise that. I can't point you to research that tested any of these in bed or measured sleep, though they may help you settle. Sleep trouble that keeps coming back is worth raising with a doctor.

These practices are meant to support professional care. They don't replace it. Sleep trouble that keeps coming back is worth raising with a doctor, who can check whether something physical is behind it. If you take medication for anxiety or sleep, please talk with your doctor before changing anything.

All three exercises come from my book, Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety. It has the full 3 a.m. sequence and 27 ranked exercises, each with a note on how strong its evidence is.

author: maya-chen
title: A 10-Minute Daily Vagus Nerve Routine: Morning and Night
dek: Vagus nerve exercises daily, without a free hour: a 6-minute morning sequence at your coffee and a 4-minute wind-down at your toothbrush.
seo_title: Vagus Nerve Exercises Daily: A 10-Minute Routine
seo_description: Vagus nerve exercises daily, step by step: a 6-minute morning sequence with your coffee, a 4-minute evening wind-down, and how to keep it going.
body_html:
It's 6:52 in the morning. The kettle is starting to tick, your phone is already face up on the counter, and your chest has been tight since before you opened your eyes. Nothing has happened yet today.

If you've been looking for vagus nerve exercises daily, something small enough to survive a real morning, this is the routine from my book: 10 minutes a day, in two halves. Six minutes in the morning, stacked on your coffee, and four at night, stacked on your toothbrush. Here is the morning half in full, and how to keep both going.

Why do vagus nerve exercises daily, and not once a week?

The vagus nerve is a long nerve that links your brain with your heart, lungs and gut. Your heart speeds up slightly as you breathe in and slows slightly as you breathe out, and your vagus nerve is part of that rhythm (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014). A slow breath gives that rhythm more room, which is why slow breathing sits at the center of this routine.

The case for every day is mostly about habit. In a study of 96 people repeating a new behavior after the same daily cue, it took about 66 days on average to feel automatic (Lally et al., 2010). Picture Teresa, 39, a composite, not a real person: two meditation apps she never opens, and coffee every single morning. That's where this routine lives.

What the morning half is made of

In healthy adults, cortisol in saliva rises by 50 to 160 percent in the first 30 minutes after waking (Clow et al., 2004), a normal part of waking up. The morning half has three parts. It opens with three physiological sighs, the double inhale from two breathing exercises to calm down when you're stressed. Then comes resonance breathing: about six breaths a minute, in for 5 and out for 5. It ends with a cold splash at the sink.

Each person's best slow pace differs a little (Vaschillo et al., 2006), so six a minute is a starting point, not your personal number. Slow breathing near that pace is the core of heart rate variability biofeedback, and a 2020 review of 58 controlled studies found a small to moderate benefit, with larger effects for anxiety, though from few studies (Lehrer et al., 2020). That was biofeedback, not four minutes with a mug, so it is no promise. The cold splash has the least behind it: I have no study of a few splashes at the sink to offer, so it is optional.

Before you begin

A safety note: if you have asthma or COPD, check with your physician before practicing paced or extended breathing. If you're prone to lightheadedness or hyperventilation, go slowly and keep the counts shorter at first. If you feel dizzy, return to normal breathing right away. And if you carry trauma or tend to dissociate, breathwork can occasionally feel activating rather than settling. You can stop and breathe naturally at any point.

If focusing on your breath raises your anxiety, do just the sighs and the splash for the first week. For the cold water: if you have a heart condition, cold water on the face can slow your heart rate sharply, so check with your physician first. If you're unsure, skip putting your face in the water and splash cool, not cold, water on your face and wrists.

The 6-minute morning sequence, step by step

Stand or sit near your kitchen sink, coffee on its way.

  1. Sigh three times. Inhale fully through your nose for 4 counts, then take a second, shorter sniff on top. Exhale slowly through your mouth for 6 to 8 counts and let your shoulders drop. Do this 3 times, about 30 seconds in all, while the kettle boils.
  2. Pick up your mug. Hold it in both hands and feel the heat. This is your cue for the next step.
  3. Breathe in for 5, out for 5. Inhale through your nose for 5 counts and exhale through your nose or mouth for 5 counts. Continue for 4 minutes, about 24 breaths, feeling your belly rise and fall.
  4. Set the mug down and move to the sink.
  5. Splash. Splash cold tap water over your forehead, cheeks and the back of your neck 3 to 5 times, or put your face in a sink of water for 15 to 30 seconds if that's comfortable. Breathe out as you lift your face. About 30 seconds.
  6. Ground. Stand upright and take one slow breath. Notice how your body feels now. You don't need to feel different.

The timed steps add up to 5 minutes: 30 seconds of sighs, 4 minutes of slow breathing and about 30 seconds at the sink. The hand-offs and closing breath fill the sixth.

If sitting is uncomfortable, do the slow breathing standing at the counter or lying in bed before you get up. If the cold is too much, use cool water for the first two weeks; moving to colder water is one of the book's upgrades for week 3.

This is Exercise 4A in my book, Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety. The book adds the structure for keeping it: a page for deciding where each step goes in your morning, a 28-day log where you rate your anxiety from 0 to 5 each morning before you start, and one small upgrade at a time in weeks 3 and 4, such as 2 minutes of humming after the splash.

How the two halves make one daily vagus nerve routine

The evening half is the 4-minute wind-down at your toothbrush: 2 minutes of breathing in for 4 and out for 8 (6 if 8 feels strained) before you brush, then 2 minutes of humming while you change and dim the lights. The full steps and their safety note are in breathing exercises for sleep: the longer exhale at bedtime.

Together they make the 10 minutes. In the book, the first two weeks have one job: do both halves every day, at the same length, without stretching the breathing or pushing the water colder. Some evenings you'll forget and do the wind-down in bed, half asleep. That counts. Imperfect practice still counts.

Imperfect practice still counts.

How to keep a nervous system regulation routine going

  • Stack it on coffee. Sighs while the kettle boils, slow breathing with the mug in your hands, the splash before you get dressed.
  • Stack it on your toothbrush. Breathing just before you brush, humming just after, until the light goes off.
  • Name the moment. Before Day 1, the book asks you to finish a sentence: "Every morning, I will begin my physiological sighs at ___ in ___."
  • Keep a minimum for hard days. When you're sick, traveling or short on sleep, the book's minimum is three sighs in the morning and 2 minutes of humming before sleep.
  • Watch the week, not the day. If you use the book's log, write the number down and look at the trend each week.

What you might notice

You might yawn, sigh or shudder after the sighs, or feel a mild warmth in your chest after the slow breathing. If tingling in your hands or face grows, breathe normally for a minute before you go on.

You might also notice nothing, or feel slightly restless, especially in the first week. That's common and it doesn't mean you did it wrong. Feeling that nothing is happening is different from feeling worse: if the morning sequence keeps leaving you more anxious, stop, go back to the sighs alone, and mention it to your doctor.

When to use it

  • Right after you wake, before the phone, while the kettle heats.
  • In bed before you get up, with the slow breathing done lying down.

If you wake braced at 3 a.m. rather than at 7, try these vagus nerve exercises you can do in bed. New to all of this? Start with nervous system regulation for beginners and its 3-minute check-in.

This week, when the kettle clicks on, bring your attention to your shoulders. Take one physiological sigh before you reach for your phone. Then notice what your nervous system does.

Questions women ask about daily vagus nerve exercises

How long until I notice anything? It varies, and I can't give you a timeline. Many people notice nothing at first, which is common. The book's 0 to 5 log lets you look at weeks of numbers instead of judging one morning.

Can I do vagus nerve exercises every day? This routine is built for every day: six minutes in the morning and four at night, at the same length for the first two weeks. With a heart condition, ask your physician before the cold splash.

What if I miss a day? Start again the next morning at the usual length. On hard days, three sighs in the morning and 2 minutes of humming at night are the book's minimum. If you miss more than 3 days in a row after adding an upgrade, the book has you go back to the basic six and four first.

These practices are meant to support professional care, not replace it. If your symptoms are new or keep coming back, a doctor can check that a physical problem isn't behind them. If you take medication for anxiety, please talk with your doctor before changing anything.

The morning and evening sequences, the 28-day log and the hard-day minimum are all in Chapter 4 of my book, Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety.
